title: Two Things That Happened
theme: Telling two things that really happened
materials: No materials needed, though a photo or an object from one of the events can help.
instructions: Pick two things that happened close together and not long ago — went outside then had lunch, had a snack then played, got home then fed the cat. Ask your child to tell you about it, or start by telling your own two-event version: "First we went outside. Then we ate lunch." Pause and leave plenty of room. Accept any telling that gets both things across — "we went outside and we ate lunch" is a two-event story. Say it back warmly as one telling, and show you are interested in what happened rather than in how it was said.
success_criteria: The child tells at least TWO things that happened. The two events may come as two sentences or as one longer sentence, and words such as "first" or "then" are not required as long as both events are understandable. One event on its own is not success here — a single-event recount is the sentence-building target, not this one.
make_easier: Use two things that happened in the last few minutes. Hold an object from one of them, or show a photo. Tell your own two-event version first, or give a starter — "First we..." You can supply the first event and ask what happened after it. One event is a real step and should be warmly expanded to two, but only two events meet this target.
make_harder: Ask with no photo, no object and no model, about earlier in the day. Invite one useful detail inside one of the events — who was there, or where it was. You can also ask for a third thing that happened.
group_play_line: A sibling can tell their own two things from the same part of the day, so your child hears the shape before taking a turn.
what_to_avoid: Do not quiz for details or ask the same question again and again. Do not tell your child their memory is wrong — if the order comes out muddled, say your version back warmly and move on. Do not correct grammar while a story is being told, and never use an upsetting event as story material.

title: Two-Picture Story
theme: Telling what happened across two pictures
materials: Two pictures showing a simple sequence with the same person, animal or character — washing hands then drying them, a dog finding a ball then carrying it, a tower built then fallen over.
instructions: Put the two pictures in front of your child, left to right, and look at them together for a moment. Ask your child to tell you the story, or tell your own two-event version once: "He washed his hands. Then he dried them." Pause. Accept any telling that gets both pictures across, and say it back warmly as one story. If your child names what is in each picture instead of telling what happened, say the story version yourself and try another pair another day.
success_criteria: The child tells BOTH events out loud — what happens in the first picture and what happens in the second. Putting the pictures in the right order, pointing at them, or naming what is in them is NOT success on its own: this card is about telling the events, not about arranging or labelling them.
make_easier: Use a pair your child knows very well, and keep the two pictures clearly different from each other. Tell your own two-event version first, then ask. You can give a starter for the first picture and let your child finish it, then do the same for the second. Telling one picture is a real step; both are the target.
make_harder: Use a pair your child has not seen before. Or look at the two pictures together, set them aside, and let your child tell the story — bring them back if needed. You can add a third picture.
group_play_line: A sibling can tell the first picture and your child the second, then swap so each of them tells the whole pair.
what_to_avoid: Do not make "which one comes first?" the point of the activity — ordering is not what this practises. Do not correct grammar in the middle of a story. If your child does not want to tell it, tell it yourself and leave the pair out for later.

title: What Happened Next?
theme: Adding the second event to a story the caregiver starts
materials: No materials needed — use something familiar your child does often.
instructions: Start a tiny familiar story out loud and stop: "The boy put on his shoes, and then..." Look interested and wait. Beginning the story this way is a fine way in, and your child adding the second event is exactly the right first step. Accept any sensible next event they offer, then say the whole two-event story back as one telling: "He put on his shoes, and then he went outside." Do not ask your child to say it again after you. At another opportunity, name something familiar and invite your child to tell you the whole tiny story — both things that happened — and let them start one for you if they want to.
success_criteria: The child tells a two-event story out loud, expressing both events in words. The events may come as two sentences or as one connected sentence. A single guessed word is not enough, and the child's second event does not have to be the one you had in mind. If you supply the first event and your child supplies the second, that is useful scaffolding toward the target, but it does not yet count as full two-event narration success.
make_easier: Use something your child does every day. Offer two spoken endings to choose between — "and then he went outside, or and then he had a nap?" — and let your child answer in words. Then say the whole two-event story back, so your child keeps hearing the shape. Treat these as scaffolding toward the target rather than the target itself: when you give the first event and your child gives the second, your child has expressed one event, and what to look for at a later opportunity is your child telling both. Never ask for an immediate repetition.
make_harder: Invite your child to tell both events without choices, a starter or a model. Once that is comfortable, invite a third event or one extra detail. You can also let your child start a tiny two-event story on their own and tell the whole thing.
group_play_line: Take turns: one person starts the story and the other says what happened next.
what_to_avoid: Do not treat this as a test of guessing the right answer — any sensible event is correct. Do not keep asking if nothing comes; finish the story yourself and try again another time.

title: Tell the Toy Story
theme: Telling the story of two things the toys just did
materials: Two or three familiar toys — a teddy, a doll, a toy car, some animals.
instructions: With your child, make the toys do two simple connected things: teddy eats his dinner, then teddy goes to sleep. Or the car drives to the shop, then the car comes home. Keep it short, and let your child join in with the actions if they want to. Then stop, hold the toys still, and ask your child to tell you what happened. Accept any telling that gets both things across, and say it back warmly as one story.
success_criteria: The child tells at least TWO things the toys did. Doing the actions again, or moving the toys to show you, is not success on its own — the two events have to be told out loud.
make_easier: Use two things the toys do inside something your child knows well, and do them slowly. Tell the story yourself once, then do the actions again and ask. A starter such as "First teddy..." helps.
make_harder: Do the two actions and wait longer before asking. Or let your child decide what the toys do and then tell you about it. You can add a third thing the toys did.
group_play_line: A sibling can work the toys while your child tells the story, then they switch over.
what_to_avoid: Do not push your child into pretend play if they are not interested — the toys are a way to make two events happen, not the point of the card. Keep the actions ordinary and gentle, and do not ask for an imaginative or elaborate story.

title: My Photo Story
theme: Telling two things that happened, from family photos
materials: Two photos from the same outing or occasion — arriving somewhere then seeing something, candles on a cake then eating it, putting on a costume then going out.
instructions: Choose two photos from one occasion your child remembers and enjoyed. Look at them together. Ask your child to tell you about that day, or tell your own two-event version once: "We got to the zoo. Then we saw the elephants." Pause and leave room. Accept any telling that gets both things across, and say it back warmly. Keep the conversation about what happened rather than about who is in the picture.
success_criteria: The child tells at least TWO things that happened on that occasion. Naming the people or the things in the photos is NOT success — that is person and object naming, and this card is about telling what happened.
make_easier: Use photos from something very recent and very familiar. Tell your own two-event version first. You can supply the first event and ask what happened after it. One event is a real step; two is the target.
make_harder: Use photos from longer ago. Or look at them, put them away, and let your child tell it — bring them back if needed. Invite one detail inside an event, or ask for a third thing that happened.
group_play_line: Anyone who was there can tell their own two things from the same photos, which often reminds your child of more.
what_to_avoid: Do not use photos of anything upsetting, and do not correct your child's memory of the day — say your version warmly and let both stand. Do not work through a whole album; two photos is the whole activity.

title: Fix My Mixed-Up Story
theme: Retelling a muddled two-event story so it makes sense
materials: No materials needed — use something ordinary your child has done many times.
instructions: Tell a two-event story about something familiar with the two events the wrong way round: "We ate the sandwich, and then we made it." Look puzzled and say "That sounds silly. Tell me what really happened." Pause and give your child room. Accept any telling that puts both events into a sensible relationship, say it back warmly as one story, and try another muddled one while it is still fun.
success_criteria: The child tells BOTH events out loud in a sensible order or relationship. Saying which one came first, pointing, or just saying "no" is not success on its own — the child has to tell the two-event story.
make_easier: Use the most familiar thing you have and make the muddle obvious. After your child protests, tell the sensible version once yourself, then muddle a different one and ask again. A starter — "First we..." — helps.
make_harder: Use a muddle that is a little less obvious. Or let your child tell you a mixed-up story for you to put right, and then ask them for the real version.
group_play_line: Take turns being the one who gets the story muddled up.
what_to_avoid: Keep every mix-up playful and about ordinary things — never muddle a bedtime, medical, toileting or safety routine, and never anything your child finds important or worrying. The only thing being put right is your own silly story, never your child. Stop if your child seems confused rather than amused.

title: Make Up a Tiny Story
materials: One character and one thing — a toy dog and a ball, a teddy and a bed, a doll and a kite. Pictures work too.
instructions: Pick one character and one object, and start a story out loud: "The dog found a ball..." Pause and let your child add what happened. Accept any event they offer, then tell the whole two-event story back as one telling: "The dog found a ball, and then he took it home." Starting the story for your child is a fine way in. Across different opportunities leave more of it to your child, until the whole tiny story — both things that happened — comes from them. A plain, ordinary story is exactly right, and there is no need to ask your child to repeat it after you.
success_criteria: The child tells a made-up two-event story out loud, expressing both events in words. The story does not need to be original, clever, surprising or grammatically perfect. Both events have to be told rather than acted out. If you supply the first event and your child adds the second, that is appropriate scaffolding, but full success is recorded when your child tells both events.
make_easier: Supply the first event yourself and offer two spoken endings to choose between, with your child answering in words. Use a character and an object your child likes. Tell a whole two-event example first, so the shape is familiar. All of this is scaffolding toward the target rather than the success criterion itself: full success is your child telling both events, so across opportunities hand more of the story over.
make_harder: Let your child invent both events with no starter. Add a third event, or move from a toy character to one from a story your child already knows.
group_play_line: Build the story round the group — one person adds an event, then the next, keeping it to two or three in total.
what_to_avoid: Do not judge the story or ask for something more imaginative; inventiveness is not what this practises. Do not insist on finishing a story your child has lost interest in.
